clue.text: Feel the loss of planet’s great beauty

blocks.note: to miss someone is to feel their absence
our planet is the world

explanation.surface: Someone mourns the passing of the most beautiful thing on Earth.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as a possessive but works as 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The title goes to the winner of an international beauty pageant, so its holder is by definition a celebrated beauty.

clue.text: Minute horse enters frightening collection of animals

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: M is the standard abbreviation for minute
something frightening is eerie
a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: A tiny horse wanders into a scary zoo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute' looks like an adjective for the horse, but it is the time unit, abbreviated to its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A menagerie is a collection of wild or unusual creatures kept for exhibition, historically in a private travelling show.

clue.text: Intuition not immediately arousing love?

definitions.note: a cryptic description, the opposite of love at first sight

blocks.note: first meaning: the supposed ability to perceive what is not visible
second meaning, playful: love that arrives at the next look rather than the first

explanation.surface: A hunch that doesn't spark instant romance.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: if love at first sight is immediate, love that takes another look comes at the next sighting.
explanation.definitionFit: Clairvoyance or uncanny perception is called by this phrase, a close relative of intuition or a sixth sense.

clue.text: Cry of excitement before learner makes turn

blocks.note: 'whee!' is a cry of glee, as on a slide
L stands for learner, as on L-plates

explanation.surface: A learner driver yelps with excitement before swinging round a corner.
explanation.walkthrough: L-plates are the red-on-white signs a British learner driver must display.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to wheel means to pivot or swing round, as soldiers or birds do, so it works as a synonym.

clue.text: Mount and gallop even faster

blocks.note: to gallop is to rush
doing even more of it, i.e. faster

explanation.surface: A rider gets on a horse and spurs it on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' seems to mean climb onto a horse, but it is the title of a mountain, read as a proper name.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Rushmore in South Dakota is the peak carved with four presidential heads, so the name fills the gap after 'Mount'.

clue.text: Lower classes are not able to handle wine

blocks.note: D and E are the lowest grades in the British social classification
'are not able' is can't

explanation.surface: Snobbish complaint that working-class people don't know how to serve wine.
explanation.walkthrough: British market research grades households A, B, C1, C2, D and E, so the lower classes are D and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Pouring wine off its sediment into a carafe is the standard way of serving an older bottle, the classic act of wine service.

clue.text: Diocese was perhaps making this condition?

indicators.note: the answer's own first word is the signal: the letters go crazy and are remade into another order

blocks.note: the answer's first word, which acts as the instruction for the rest
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bishop's whole diocese seems to have caught some strange affliction.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as an instruction: 'Diocese was', mad (jumbled), gives the remaining two words. The clue's wordplay points back at itself.
explanation.definitionFit: BSE, the bovine brain illness of the 1980s and 90s, is a medical condition in cattle known popularly by this name.

clue.text: Be irritated by bookworm, one of unusual sense

blocks.note: to mind something is to object to it
a bookworm is a keen reader

explanation.surface: Someone finds a bookish person annoying, and that person seems oddly perceptive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mind' as in 'do you mind?' means to be bothered by something.
explanation.definitionFit: A telepath supposedly has an extra faculty for knowing thoughts, a sense beyond the ordinary five.

clue.text: Airport outlet where staff have nothing to do?

definitions.text: where staff have nothing to do
definitions.note: a playful description of a workplace

blocks.note: first meaning: the tax-exempt store past security

blocks.clueFragment: where staff have nothing to do
blocks.note: second meaning, punning: a shop where workers are released from all obligations

explanation.surface: A sleepy airport store where the assistants stand around idle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duty' here means tax, not work obligation; the question mark signals the pun on being free of duties.
explanation.definitionFit: Airports have stores selling goods exempt from import tax to international travellers, a standard outlet type.

clue.text: Notice paper has run out

indicators.note: something that has gone out is no longer there, so a letter leaves

blocks.note: A British Sunday newspaper
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A newspaper notice saying the paper's supply has been exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer is the world's oldest Sunday newspaper, published in London.
explanation.definitionFit: To notice something is to see or perceive it, and the verb here is a direct synonym for that act of perception.

clue.text: How to make t-those old clothes

blocks.note: first meaning, a cryptic recipe: write one letter twice, then follow it with a word for stockings, and you get the stammered word
second meaning: the jacket and tights worn by men in Tudor times

explanation.surface: A stammering tailor explains how to sew some old garments.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter spells t-t-hose: a doubled T followed by HOSE, and that recipe names Elizabethan menswear.
explanation.definitionFit: A close jacket and tights were the standard male costume of Tudor and Elizabethan England, now seen as old-fashioned dress.

clue.text: Serious, regular gaps in tummy bone

indicators.note: gaps at even intervals mean every other letter is skipped and only the alternate ones kept

blocks.note: stern means grave or serious
the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A grave remark about gaps in the bones of the belly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tummy bone' looks like a single phrase, but the definition is the last word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The breastbone in the middle of the chest is known anatomically by this Latin name; it is a flat bone joining the ribs.

clue.text: Omen certain to disturb seat of empire

indicators.note: disturbing something throws it out of its settled order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A soothsayer's sign is sure to unsettle an emperor's throne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seat' suggests a throne, but it means the capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: The classical city was the capital and administrative centre of the Roman Empire, so it was the empire's seat.

clue.text: Man entitled ahead of time to stop short

indicators.note: stopping short means finishing before the end, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: arriving ahead of time is arriving early

explanation.surface: A man claims the right to cut things off before the scheduled time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entitled' seems to mean having a right, but here it means holding a title of nobility.
explanation.definitionFit: This British nobleman ranks between viscount and marquess, a man with a hereditary title.

clue.text: Tin backed by engineers as a valuable natural substance

indicators.note: turned back to front, so these letters run the other way

blocks.note: a tin is a can
RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps

explanation.surface: Tin, financed by engineers, treated as a precious natural material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tin' looks like the metal, which fits 'natural substance', but it is a container; the RE are the Royal Engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: Mother-of-pearl, the iridescent lining of shells, is prized in jewellery and inlay, a precious organic material.

clue.text: Certificates nobody in the office has?

definitions.text: Certificates nobody in the office has?

blocks.clueFragment: Certificates nobody in the office has?
blocks.note: surface reading: qualifications that none of the staff possesses

blocks.clueFragment: Certificates nobody in the office has?
blocks.note: setter's reading: the papers that explain why nobody is at their desk, everyone being off ill

explanation.surface: A boss laments that nobody on the staff holds any qualifications.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'nobody in the office' as an empty office: the certificates are what everyone has handed in to explain their absence.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a doctor's certificate excusing an employee from work through illness is informally called by this name.

clue.text: One formerly driven to organise crusade

indicators.note: organising things puts them into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A former zealot is pushed into leading a holy war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driven' suggests someone motivated, but it means a vehicle steered by a previous owner.
explanation.definitionFit: A second-hand vehicle has already had an owner who drove it, which the definition describes with deliberate ambiguity.

clue.text: For film, polite folk like to choose the lighter sort

blocks.note: gentlemen are courteous, well-mannered people
to prefer is to like better and choose
blondes are those with fair, lighter hair

explanation.surface: Well-mannered people at the cinema opt for something less heavy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The lighter sort' suggests a frothier film, but it means fair-haired people.
explanation.definitionFit: This 1953 musical comedy starring Marilyn Monroe and Jane Russell is a famous Hollywood picture.

clue.text: Very many thanks at end of tour for guide

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, which is all that is kept

blocks.note: loads means a great many
ta is British informal for thanks
its final letter

explanation.surface: A tourist thanks the guide warmly when the trip is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guide' looks like the tour guide being thanked, but it is the definition: a star steered by. 'Ta' is everyday British slang for thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: The pole star was used by navigators to steer, so the word came to mean anything that serves as a guiding principle.

clue.text: A woman holding other people briefly in her prayers?

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a rosary is a sequence of prayers counted on beads
'em is a shortened them, i.e. other people

explanation.surface: A woman keeps others in her prayers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding someone in your prayers' is an idiom for praying for them, which disguises the container; 'em is the clipped them.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a girl's name, so it stands for a woman in the same way any female forename does in crosswords.

clue.text: Government facility: a police station?

blocks.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police
a station or post can be an office

explanation.surface: Is a police station counted as a public facility?
explanation.walkthrough: The Met Office is Britain's national weather service, a government agency; the Met is also the London police force.
explanation.definitionFit: The UK's state meteorological agency is run by the government, making it a public body providing a service.

clue.text: Many happy returns for MP here?

definitions.text: Many happy returns for MP here?

blocks.note: surface reading: a birthday greeting to a member of parliament

blocks.clueFragment: Many happy returns for MP here
blocks.note: setter's reading: a constituency that sends the same politician back to parliament election after election

explanation.surface: Birthday wishes for a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returns' means being returned to parliament at an election, not birthdays.
explanation.definitionFit: A constituency where one party's majority is so large the member is reliably re-elected is called this in British politics.

clue.text: Mark maybe Bismarck’s watchword

blocks.note: M abbreviates the mark, the old German currency
Otto von Bismarck was the German chancellor

explanation.surface: Perhaps a German currency symbol was the Iron Chancellor's slogan.
explanation.walkthrough: Bismarck's first name supplies the letters; the apostrophe-s is 'is', linking to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A slogan or maxim adopted as a guiding rule is a watchword, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Shares fish, relaxing here after swim?

blocks.note: to pool resources is to share them
the ide is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: Someone shares out fish while lounging after a dip.
explanation.walkthrough: The ide, a European carp, is a crossword regular; 'here' points to a place.
explanation.definitionFit: After a swim, people lie on loungers on the deck beside the water, so this area is where they unwind.

clue.text: From peak, leader drops right back, nowhere near podium finish

indicators.note: the front letter falls all the way to the rear, rotating the word by one place

blocks.note: a peak is a height, a high point

explanation.surface: A climber falls from the summit, ending far down the field.
explanation.walkthrough: Move the opening letter of the word for a peak to the end. 'Right back' sounds like a footballer's position but means all the way to the rear.
explanation.definitionFit: A podium holds the first three finishers, so coming in at position number eight is well outside the medals.

clue.text: Put up with a south wind? Not that one

blocks.note: to bear, past tense bore, is to put up with
taken as written
S is the compass abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: Someone tolerates a southerly breeze, then corrects themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a wind, but 'Not that one' warns it is not the southerly one: it is the north wind.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek mythology this god personified the cold north wind, the opposite of a southern breeze.

clue.text: Confessed end of working week not always filled with love and calmness

indicators.note: a negative strips away whatever follows it, so those letters are removed
a thing filled with something has it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: to sing is slang for confessing to the police
the last day of the working week
ay (or aye) is an old word for always, ever
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A worker admitted that Fridays are not always full of love and serenity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sang' is underworld slang for informing; 'ay' meaning always is archaic and a crossword favourite. Take it from the weekday, then put the zero inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase literally 'cold blood' means composure under pressure, a synonym for calmness.

clue.text: To establish part of argument may be an advantage in court

blocks.note: to set something up is to establish it
an argument is made up of points

explanation.surface: A lawyer making a point to gain an edge in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a law court, but it is a tennis court.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis, a player one rally away from winning the set holds this, a clear lead at that moment.

clue.text: Put into shape, since tangled

blocks.note: for can mean since or because
matted hair is tangled

explanation.surface: Something was knocked into shape because it had become knotted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tangled' looks like an anagram signal, but it supplies letters by meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: To format a document is to arrange it in a set layout, giving it its structure or shape.

clue.text: Woman in work: one having conversation on-line?

blocks.note: first meaning: the heroine of a famous D H Lawrence novel
second meaning, a pun: a lady chatting on a ley, a mystical line across the landscape

explanation.surface: A woman at the office chats away on the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the name as LADY + CHATTER + LEY: a ley line is a supposed alignment of ancient sites. 'On-line' is not the internet.
explanation.definitionFit: Constance, the title character of Lawrence's banned-then-famous 1928 novel, is a woman in a literary work.

clue.text: Obtain file with trickery: that should be reported

indicators.note: trickery manipulates and rearranges, so the letters are juggled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Getting hold of a document by deception is something to report.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a crime to report; the definition is the last phrase alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A disease or offence that must legally be declared to the authorities is described with this adjective.

clue.text: This book isn’t one of the Ruritanian series? No chance!

definitions.text: This book isn’t one of the Ruritanian series

blocks.clueFragment: This book isn’t one of the Ruritanian series
blocks.note: first meaning: Anthony Hope wrote the Ruritania novels, so a book not by him is not one of his
second meaning: an emphatic refusal or dismissal of the possibility

explanation.surface: A librarian dismisses the idea that this volume belongs to a famous adventure series.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Hope wrote The Prisoner of Zenda, set in the imaginary kingdom of Ruritania.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an informal British way of saying something is impossible or utterly unlikely.

clue.text: Engine lacking constant temperature for haul

indicators.note: lacking something means being without it, so a letter goes

blocks.note: loco is short for locomotive, a railway engine
c is the symbol for a constant, such as the speed of light
T is the symbol for temperature

explanation.surface: A train without steady heat can't pull its load.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haul' suggests a locomotive pulling, but it is a noun: a thief's takings.
explanation.definitionFit: A haul is a quantity of stolen goods, and stolen goods are plunder, the synonym here.

clue.text: Endlessly tough surgeon seizes top of scalpel for period of cutting

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is chopped off
the top of a word in an across clue is its first letter
to seize is to grab and hold, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: tough means hard
a vet is an animal surgeon
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A hard-nosed surgeon grabs a scalpel for an operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting' suggests surgery, but the cutting is of crops.
explanation.definitionFit: The season when crops are reaped and gathered in involves cutting the grain, so it is a time of cutting.

clue.text: Detectives suppress vice among more corrupt band of heralds

indicators.note: to suppress is to hold down and contain, so one piece is held inside
being among things puts it in their midst, so it goes inside

blocks.note: bent is slang for corrupt, so more corrupt is benter
DIs are detective inspectors
a vice is a sin

explanation.surface: Police cover up wrongdoing among crooked colleagues.
explanation.walkthrough: Put the vice inside the detectives after their first letter, then put that inside the comparative of bent. 'Heralds' are experts in coats of arms, not messengers.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry, a diagonal stripe running from upper right to lower left of a shield, traditionally linked with illegitimacy, is this charge.

clue.text: On reflection silly lisp — I tick boxes like being drunk

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so the answer sits inside other words
a reflection in a mirror runs the other way

blocks.note: the letters spanning the word breaks

explanation.surface: Someone thinks back: a daft slur and ticking boxes are signs of drunkenness.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards through 'sillY LISP I Tick' and the answer appears; a slurred lisp suits the drunken surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb describes doing something in a slightly drunk way, as a tipsy person would.

clue.text: In leaving the racetrack, rake creates spinning

indicators.note: a word placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: a racing car leaves the track to go into the pits, which is pitting
a roué is a rake, a dissolute man

explanation.surface: A playboy spins out as he leaves the race circuit.
explanation.walkthrough: In motor racing, pitting is pulling off the track into the pit lane; 'rake' is a womaniser, not a garden tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A pirouette is a ballet turn on one foot, so the verb form describes whirling round in place.

clue.text: Rejecting sexually ambivalent old goat

indicators.note: rejecting something sends it back the way it came

blocks.note: bi is short for bisexual
ex means former

explanation.surface: Spurning an ageing, sexually undecided lecher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old goat' reads as an insult for a lecherous man, but 'old' is wordplay and the definition is the last word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: This wild mountain animal with long curved horns lives in the Alps and is a species of wild goat.

clue.text: Just a two-course meal could be an unacceptable idea

blocks.note: first meaning, a pun: a dinner of main and pudding, skipping the first course
second meaning: a proposal with no chance of succeeding

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses the suggestion of a scaled-back dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the first course of a meal is the starter, so a two-course meal may lack one.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan or proposal that is doomed from the outset is called this, from a horse that never begins a race.

clue.text: Do survey in pouring rain and gale? Tut!

indicators.note: pouring liquid sloshes and mixes, so the letters tumble into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, leaving out 'and'

explanation.surface: A surveyor tuts at having to work in a downpour and high wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pouring' fits the weather picture perfectly but it is the anagram signal; 'and' just joins the two weather words.
explanation.definitionFit: Surveyors fix positions by measuring angles from known points, forming triangles; the verb names that measuring method.

clue.text: Brain cells struggling to identify plant

indicators.note: something struggling is in disarray and out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone racks their brains trying to name a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a gardener's memory lapse; the definition is the final word.
explanation.definitionFit: The wild geranium, with beak-shaped seed pods, is a flowering garden species known by this common name.

clue.text: Henry and Rose arranged to drive off for hearing: it may bring them luck

indicators.note: arranging puts items into a fresh order
what is heard is the sound, not the spelling

blocks.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
taken as written
shoo is what you say to drive away a cat or bird

explanation.surface: A couple, Henry and Rose, set off on a drive in search of good luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Henry and Rose' look like two people, but Henry is the physics unit. 'Them' at the end refers back to whoever owns the charm.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved iron horse's shoe hung over a door is a traditional good-luck charm in Britain and elsewhere.

clue.text: Man fired by bureaucrat with good courage

indicators.note: someone fired is dismissed and leaves, so those letters go

blocks.note: a mandarin is a senior civil servant
taken as written
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: An employee is sacked by an official, and good nerve is called for.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a powerful senior civil servant is called a mandarin, after imperial Chinese officials.
explanation.definitionFit: Boldness or the willingness to take risks is a form of bravery, so the noun is a synonym for courage.

clue.text: Hall a great success, but no place to get a drink

indicators.note: 'but no' means without, so those letters are excluded

blocks.note: a great success is a triumph
PH is the abbreviation for public house, a pub

explanation.surface: A village hall event went well, though there was no bar.
explanation.walkthrough: PH marks a pub on British maps, so 'place to get a drink' supplies two letters to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: An open central court or lofty entrance space in a building serves as a hall or lobby.

clue.text: Why not take an extra month?

blocks.note: first meaning: a resigned agreement that there is no reason against it
second meaning, a pun: have the fifth month of the year in addition

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs and suggests extending a holiday by a month.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'may' as the calendar month: taking it as well means taking an extra month.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying there is no good reason against something is the shrug of 'why not?', an idiom of reluctant assent.

clue.text: Half encourage a creative spirit

blocks.note: demi- is a prefix meaning half
to urge is to encourage

explanation.surface: Someone half-heartedly encourages an artistic person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creative spirit' sounds like an artist, but it is a divine maker in philosophy.
explanation.definitionFit: In Platonic and Gnostic thought, the divine craftsman who fashions the physical world is a creative being.

clue.text: Quietly swelling, becoming this?

blocks.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning quietly
a lump is a swelling

explanation.surface: A person putting on weight gradually, without anyone noticing.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: swelling quietly is how someone gets round. The wordplay sits in the first two words, and 'becoming this' points at the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Gradually filling out in body leaves a person rounded and slightly fat, which is the adjective's meaning.

clue.text: Pressure to reconsider, getting a peek ahead

blocks.note: p is the symbol for pressure
to review something is to reconsider it

explanation.surface: Pressure to rethink a decision brings an early glimpse of things.
explanation.walkthrough: P for pressure is the physics symbol, a standard crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An advance showing, such as a film screened before release, gives an early look at what is coming.

clue.text: So tennis involved strains

indicators.note: something involved is complicated and tangled up

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Playing tennis led to pulled muscles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strains' looks like muscle injuries from sport, but here it means pressures or stresses.
explanation.definitionFit: Stresses or pulls, physical or emotional, are synonyms for the plural noun here.

clue.text: A misplaced lamb stew turns up: bliss!

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up runs the letters from bottom to top
one letter is put in the wrong spot, a small rearrangement

blocks.note: navarin is a French stew of lamb or mutton

explanation.surface: A lost lamb casserole reappears, to great delight.
explanation.walkthrough: Write the French stew upwards, then shift one of its A's along a place.
explanation.definitionFit: In Buddhism this is the state of perfect peace and release from suffering, hence any supreme happiness.

clue.text: A teacher enters bank, but not for change

indicators.note: entering means going inside something

blocks.note: to bank on is to rely on
taken as written
a don is a university teacher

explanation.surface: A teacher goes into a bank but not to change money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' suggests currency exchange, but it means editing a file; 'bank' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: A computer file that can be viewed but not edited or altered is marked with this label.

clue.text: Twice gallon bottles ruin pointer

indicators.note: to bottle something is to shut it inside

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for gallon, taken twice
to undo something can mean to ruin it

explanation.surface: Two gallons of liquor bring about someone's downfall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointer' sounds like an arrow or tip, but it is a breed of dog used in shooting.
explanation.definitionFit: A pointer is a breed that freezes to indicate game for hunters, one type of sporting dog used with guns.

clue.text: There’s a drought; the teapot works, though, as the saying goes

annotation.answer: IT NEVER RAINS BUT IT POURS

blocks.note: a drought is a long time with no rainfall
though means but
a working teapot dispenses its tea

explanation.surface: Despite the dry spell, at least we can still make tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Each half of the proverb is taken literally: no rain, yet the teapot still does its job.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb means misfortunes come together in bunches, and it is a familiar English saying.

clue.text: Director wants one to go through storyline

indicators.note: going through something means being in its middle

blocks.note: a plot is a storyline
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A film director asks an actor to run through the story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Director' looks like a film-maker, but it is someone who steers a ship or aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's or aircraft's navigator steers and guides its course, directing where the craft goes.

clue.text: A neighbour’s ID, about a half incomplete

definitions.note: read as 'a neighbour of ID', i.e. of Idaho

indicators.note: incomplete means only part is used, so a stretch of letters is lifted out

blocks.note: the letters across the word boundaries

explanation.surface: Someone's ID card shows a figure roughly halved.
explanation.walkthrough: ID is the postal code for Idaho, so the definition is a state bordering it; the answer runs through 'abOUT A Half'.
explanation.definitionFit: The state lies directly south of Idaho, sharing a border with it, so it is one of Idaho's neighbours.

clue.text: One against entering legal process of no account

indicators.note: entering means going inside something

blocks.note: a trial is a legal hearing
I is the Roman numeral for one
v is short for versus, against

explanation.surface: A lone objector joins a court case that turns out to be pointless.
explanation.walkthrough: V for versus is how court cases are named, as in Smith v Jones, fitting the legal surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Something of little importance or significance is unimportant and petty, a synonym for having no consequence.

clue.text: Achieve reversal of revolutionary loss of rights

indicators.note: a reversal turns things back to front

blocks.note: to attain is to achieve
a red is a revolutionary communist

explanation.surface: Overturning a rebel's forfeiture of civil rights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reversal' seems to mean overturning a sentence, but it is an instruction on the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically in English law, a person condemned for treason forfeited property and civil rights by this legal penalty.

clue.text: Permission to stick head out

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, and putting it out removes it

blocks.note: to cleave to something is to stick fast to it

explanation.surface: Asking to be allowed to lean out of the window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick head out' reads as poking your head out; in fact 'cleave' means stick, and its head is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Leave is formal permission or consent, as when a court grants leave to appeal or a soldier is granted time off.

indicators.note: a chemical reaction recombines elements into something new

taken as written

explanation.surface: A bored young woman shrugs as the traffic police show up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reacts with' reads as describing the girl's attitude but is the anagram signal, mixing the words on both sides.
explanation.definitionFit: In the US, state police units that enforce road laws on major routes are known by this name.

clue.text: Royal authentication left beside ocean?

blocks.note: an ocean is a vast expanse of salt water
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A royal mark of approval placed next to the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are taken in reverse order from the clue: the ocean comes first, then the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: The monarch's official wax stamp on state documents shows the sovereign's approval of important documents.
